To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) for large proteins, the yield of molecular species increases dramatically with increasing electron energy; 2) for large proteins (> 10 k Da), multiple ionization is possible; 3) for protein–molecule complex ions, multiple ionizations occur without the dissociation of noncovalent bonds; and 4) for proteins, the fragmentation of backbone amide bonds occurs at low electron energies.

1) for proteins larger than 10 kDa, multiple ionization occurs in collisions with electrons with energy higher than 40 eV; 2) the multiple ionization of protein–molecule complex leads to fragmentation of the protein backbone and not to the dissociation of the complex; and 3) the multiple ionizations of protein–molecules complexes occur with the preservation of elements of the tertiary structure of the proteins and the weak interactions between the protein and molecule.

(1) for large biomolecules, multiple ionization by electrons can occur without the formation of molecular ions, (2) multiple ionization can also occur for intact protein–molecule (holo)complexes, and (3) for such complexes, backbone fragmentation can occur without loss of the noncovalent molecule, and such fragments can preserve the tertiary structure of the polypeptide chain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the soft ionization of biomolecules by electrons and with the fragmentation of such ions.
the soft ionization of biomolecules and their complexes in the gas phase by electron impact.
the ionization of gasphase biomolecules and their fragmentation by electrons and other soft ionization techniques.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of electrons with energy above 40 e V is a soft-ionization technique, which is applicable to large biomolecules and their complexes.
the ionization of large molecules by 70 eV EI is not “soft” in the sense of the preservation of intact molecular ions, but it is soft in terms of the low fragmentation of the polypeptide backbone.
the ionization of biomolecules by electrons is a complex and fascinating process that is not yet fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
multiple ionization of gasphase proteins and swift backbone fragmentation are both possible.

, for the first time, it is now possible to obtain multiply charged ions for large (> 10kDa) biomolecules by electron ionization, and that the fragmentation of such ions is dominated by backbone fragmentation, that is, by the cleavage of the amide bonds in the polypeptide chains.
, in collisions with low-energy electrons, protein ions can increase their charge by one unit, whereas with higher-energy electrons, the charge state of proteins can be doubled.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ionization of large biomolecules with electrons can be a soft process, and the subsequent fragmentation of the molecular ion can be directed towards the backbone.
, with a sufficiently large electron flux, multiple ionization of proteins can be achieved with a low probability of backbone fragmentation.
the use of higher-energy electrons in the EI process can produce intact molecular ions of larger biomolecules and that such species can retain their native structure in the gas phase.
